    <cue id="scene-3-cue">
      <voice>Breaking in needed skilled people, expensive tools, and patience, so the most capable attackers went after banks, governments, and giant corporations. The rest of us were protected by something unglamorous: we were not worth the trouble.</voice>
    </cue>

More attempts, more patience, probes that run continuously and go deeper than before.</voice>

      <voice>Second, the threat has spread. The tools that help the rest of us write and research now help attackers find targets, write convincing lures, and keep trying at almost no cost. Attacks that once needed a skilled team can now be run by ordinary criminals, against everyone: your business, your accounts, your family's computers.</voice>

    <cue id="scene-6-cue">
      <voice>AI helps the attacker more than it helps the rest of us.  The balance of power is shifting in their favor because it's cheaper and easier to attack than it is to defend.  But AI can help us too.</voice>

      <voice>So what do we do? Part of the answer is old advice that suddenly matters more — and we will get to it. But part of it is new: defenders need the same advantage. If attackers use AI to scale up, defenders need AI to keep watch — reading more, remembering more, and turning what it learns into steps a person can actually take. That is the idea this publication is built on.</voice>

    <cue id="scene-8-cue">
      <voice>Behind these videos is an automated newsroom. Around the clock it monitors security research, incident reports, and newly disclosed vulnerabilities, building a structured, semantic knowledge base — attackers, tools, weaknesses, fixes — and using machine learning to watch how threats trend over time. The experts who steer it have spent their careers managing data at scale, and securing enterprise cloud environments for some of the largest companies in the world -- and getting attacked in every possible way. We use agentic AI to infer trends in knowledge bases, like the one powering our newsroom.  Instead of generating derivative AI slop summarizing secondhand headlines about best practices, our reporter agents are constantly using Charlie Munger's inversion technique to ask: How could we screw this up? How could this go wrong?  What are the failure modes that matter?  We already have handbooks of best practices.  What we need as the landscape shifts is a roadmap of the new ways that everything could go wrong.  The old, known ways that are more common or more dangerous now.</voice>
    </cue>
